notes.statement: Calakos et al. (2010) identified a novel TOR1A missense variant (c.613T-A, F205I) in a man with late-onset oromandibular focal dystonia. The variant affected a highly conserved residue in the AAA domain and was not found in 800 population controls (1,600 chromosomes). The authors suggested that the variant may contribute to the expression of dystonia.
quotes: This variant was not identified in 800 anonymized population controls (1600 chromosomes).
The phenylalanine at position 205 is highly conserved across species and is part of a highly conserved beta strand motif in the AAA domain (Figure 1B).
Together these findings raise the possibility that this novel TOR1A variant may contribute to the expression of dystonia.

notes.statement: Calakos et al. (2010) found that, in transfected BHK cells, F205I TOR1A-EGFP produced inclusions in 44% of cells, compared with 79% for deltaE TOR1A and 10% for wildtype. Unlike the deltaE inclusions, which colocalized with the nuclear envelope marker LaminB1, the larger F205I inclusions colocalized mainly with the ER marker KDEL. The authors suggested that the F205I and deltaE mutations do not have identical pathophysiology.
quotes: F205I-TOR1A-EGFP frequently produced inclusions in transfected cells (44% F205I vs. 10% wildtype; p<0.05).

F205I mutant TOR1A, in contrast to the pronounced colocalization of ΔE TOR1A with nuclear envelope markers, preferentially colocalized with the ER marker, KDEL (96%, n=67 cells) relative to Lamin B1 (19%, n=41 cells).
an observation that suggests the novel mutant TOR1A may not cause identical pathophysiology as the ΔE mutant.

notes.statement: Carbon et al. (2009) used [11C]raclopride PET to study manifesting and nonmanifesting DYT1 and DYT6 mutation carriers. Compared with healthy controls, both groups of carriers had significantly lower D2 receptor availability in the caudate and putamen (p < 0.001). The reduction was larger in DYT6 carriers than in DYT1 carriers (-38.0% vs -15.0%), and manifesting and nonmanifesting carriers of either genotype did not differ significantly.
quotes: Significant reductions in caudate and putamen D(2) receptor availability were evident in both groups of mutation carriers relative to healthy controls (p < 0.001). The changes were greater in DYT6 relative to DYT1 carriers (-38.0 +/- 3.0% vs -15.0 +/- 3.0%, p < 0.001).
By contrast, there was no significant difference between manifesting and nonmanifesting carriers of either genotype.

notes.statement: In a voxel-based analysis, Carbon et al. (2009) also found reduced raclopride binding in the ventrolateral thalamus of both DYT1 and DYT6 carriers. The reduction was more pronounced in DYT6 carriers and did not depend on whether carriers had clinical signs. The authors concluded that the reduced D2 receptor availability fits with dysfunction or loss of D2-bearing neurons, increased synaptic dopamine, or both, and that it likely represents a susceptibility factor for developing clinical manifestations.
quotes: Voxel-based analysis confirmed these findings and additionally revealed reduced RAC binding in the ventrolateral thalamus of both groups of mutation carriers.
Reduced D(2) receptor availability in carriers of dystonia genes is compatible with dysfunction or loss of D(2)-bearing neurons, increased synaptic dopamine levels, or both.
are likely to represent susceptibility factors for the development of clinical manifestations in mutation carriers.

notes.statement: Contarino et al. (2008) described a large Dutch family from a small village on a former island with autosomal dominant-appearing mild cranio-cervical-brachial focal dystonia, with 8 definitely affected and 4 possibly affected members and a mean age at onset of 45.5 years (range, 39-56). Mutations in the DYT1 and SGCE genes were not detected, and linkage to the DYT6, DYT7, DYT13, and DYT16 loci was excluded.
quotes: Eight definitely affected and four possibly affected subjects were detected. Clinical presentation consisted of mild cranio-cervical-brachial dystonia. Mean age at onset was 45.5 years (range, 39-56).
Mutations in DYT1 gene and in the epsilon-sarcoglycan (SGCE) genes were not detected. We could not find linkage to the dominant DYT6, DYT7, DYT13, or the recessive DYT16 loci.

notes.statement: Kamm et al. (2008) reported that susceptibility to DYT1 dystonia in European patients was modified by the D216H polymorphism.
quotes: Susceptibility to DYT1 dystonia in European patients is modified by the D216H polymorphism.

notes.statement: Zirn et al. (2008) found that the TOR1A p.Arg288Gln change was absent from 1000 control chromosomes and that arginine at position 288 has been conserved throughout vertebrate evolution; they concluded it may be a novel pathogenic TOR1A mutation in DYT1.
quotes: The base change is absent in 1000 control chromosomes; an Arg at position 288 of TOR1A has been conserved throughout vertebrate evolution, indicating an important role of Arg288 in TOR1A function

notes.statement: Zirn et al. (2008) found that HEK293 cells overexpressing TOR1A carrying p.Arg288Gln had an enlarged perinuclear space. Cells overexpressing the common delta-GAG mutation showed the same change, but cells overexpressing wildtype TOR1A did not.
quotes: functional studies demonstrate enlarged perinuclear space in HEK293 cells overexpressing TOR1A with the p.Arg288Gln mutation. The same morphological changes are observed in cells overexpressing the common triangle upGAG TOR1A mutation but not in cells overexpressing wild-type TOR1A.

notes.statement: In a nationwide census of French TOR1A mutation carriers, Frédéric et al. (2008) estimated the disease frequency of early-onset torsion dystonia due to TOR1A at 0.13 per 100,000 and the mutation frequency at 0.17 per 100,000, showing that the disease is rare in France.
quotes: This study demonstrates the scarcity of this disease in France with estimated disease frequency of 0.13:100,000 and mutation frequency of 0.17:100,000.

notes.statement: Frédéric et al. (2008) found the previously reported Ashkenazi Jewish haplotype in 11 of 53 French families with the TOR1A mutation. The remaining families had distinct haplotypes, which suggested independent mutation events.
quotes: The previously reported Ashkenazi-Jewish haplotype was found in 11 families with the remainder carrying distinct haplotypes suggesting independent mutation events.

notes.statement: Risch et al. (2007) studied 119 DYT1 GAG-deletion carriers with dystonia, 113 carriers without dystonia, and 197 controls. Compared with controls, the 216H allele was more frequent in carriers without dystonia and less frequent in carriers with dystonia. Haplotype analysis showed that the H allele was highly protective when in trans with the GAG deletion, and gave suggestive evidence that the D216 allele in cis is needed for the disease to be penetrant.
quotes: found the frequency of the 216H allele to be increased in GAG-deletion carriers without dystonia and to be decreased in carriers with dystonia, compared with the control individuals

Analysis of haplotypes demonstrated a highly protective effect of the H allele in trans with the GAG deletion; there was also suggestive evidence that the D216 allele in cis is required for the disease to be penetrant.

notes.statement: Risch et al. (2007) noted that the GAG deletion in DYT1 is a major cause of early-onset dystonia but that only 30% of mutation carriers develop the disease.
quotes: A GAG deletion in the DYT1 gene is a major cause of early-onset dystonia, but clinical disease expression occurs in only 30% of mutation carriers.

notes.statement: Kostić et al. (2006) described a large Serbian family with the DYT1 GAG deletion in which the phenotype varied from asymptomatic carrier status to late-onset focal dystonia and generalized jerky dystonia; of 7 mutation carriers, only 2 were affected, giving a penetrance of 29%.
quotes: We describe a large Serbian family with significant intrafamilial variability of the DYT1 phenotype, from asymptomatic carrier status to late-onset focal, and generalized jerky dystonia.
Seven mutation carriers (six proven by direct analysis and one by inferred haplotype) were identified, but only two of them were affected by dystonia (penetrance reduced to 29%).

notes.statement: In the same family, Kostić et al. (2006) found 3 GAG-deletion-negative members who also developed dystonia (2 multifocal dystonia, 1 torticollis), suggesting that their movements were due to another etiologic factor, such as another dystonia gene, or may be psychogenic.
quotes: In addition, three GAG-deletion-negative family members also developed dystonia (two multifocal dystonia and one torticollis), suggesting that their involuntary movements are due to some other etiological factor(s) (i.e., another dystonia gene), or may be psychogenic.

notes.statement: Asanuma et al. (2005) used PET with [11C]-raclopride to study non-manifesting carriers of the DYT1 mutation. Striatal D2 receptor binding was about 15% lower in the caudate and putamen (p < 0.005). The authors suggested that reduced striatal D2 binding is a trait feature of the DYT1 genotype.
quotes: the authors used PET and [11C]-raclopride to assess non-manifesting carriers of the DYT1 mutation. D2 receptor binding was reduced by approximately 15% in caudate and putamen (p < 0.005)
These results suggest that striatal D2 binding reductions are a trait feature of the DYT1 genotype.

notes.statement: Shashidharan et al. (2005) generated 4 independent lines of transgenic mice overexpressing human DeltaE-torsinA under a neuron-specific enolase promoter. About 40% of transgenic mice from each line developed abnormal involuntary movements with dystonic-appearing self-clasping of limbs as early as 3 weeks after birth, along with hyperkinesia and rapid bidirectional circling.
quotes: We generated four independent lines of transgenic mice by overexpressing human DeltaE-torsinA using a neuron specific enolase promoter.

The transgenic mice developed abnormal involuntary movements with dystonic-appearing, self-clasping of limbs, as early as 3 weeks after birth. Animals also showed hyperkinesia and rapid bi-directional circling.
Approximately 40% of transgenic mice from each line demonstrated these severe behavioral abnormalities.

notes.statement: Shashidharan et al. (2005) found decreased striatal dopamine in affected DeltaE-torsinA transgenic mice but increased levels in transgenic mice without behavioral changes. Perinuclear inclusions and aggregates staining for ubiquitin, torsinA, and lamin were found in neurons of the pedunculopontine nucleus and other brainstem regions, in a pattern similar to that described in DYT1 patients.
quotes: Neurochemical analyses revealed decreases in striatal dopamine in affected transgenic mice, although levels were increased in those that had no behavioral changes.
Immunohistochemistry demonstrated perinuclear inclusions and aggregates that stained positively for ubiquitin, torsinA and lamin, a marker of the nuclear envelope.
Inclusions were detected in neurons of the pedunculopontine nucleus and in other brain stem regions in a pattern similar to what has been described in DYT1 patients.

notes.statement: McNaught et al. (2004) found perinuclear inclusion bodies in cholinergic and other neurons of the pedunculopontine nucleus, cuneiform nucleus, and griseum centrale mesencephali in 4 genetically confirmed DYT1 patients but not in controls; the inclusions stained positively for ubiquitin, torsinA, and the nuclear envelope protein lamin A/C. They concluded that DYT1 dystonia is associated with impaired protein handling and the nuclear envelope, and suggested that alterations in these brainstem structures, which mediate motor activity and muscle tone, could underlie the pathophysiology of the disorder.
quotes: The inclusions were located within cholinergic and other neurons in the pedunculopontine nucleus, cuneiform nucleus, and griseum centrale mesencephali and stained positively for ubiquitin, torsinA, and the nuclear envelope protein lamin A/C.
This study supports the notion that DYT1 dystonia is associated with impaired protein handling and the nuclear envelope.

notes.statement: Heiman et al. (2004) gave a standardized psychiatric interview to members of families with a DYT1 mutation: 96 carriers with dystonia, 60 carriers without dystonia, and 65 noncarriers. Compared with noncarriers, the risk of recurrent major depressive disorder was higher in both non-manifesting carriers (RR = 4.95) and manifesting carriers (RR = 3.62). Carriers also developed recurrent depression at an earlier age.
quotes: mutation carriers with dystonia (manifesting carriers; n = 96), mutation carriers without dystonia (non-manifesting carriers; n = 60), and noncarriers (n = 65).

The risk for recurrent major depressive disorder was increased in both non-manifesting carriers (RR = 4.95, CI = 1.72 to 14.29) and manifesting carriers (RR = 3.62, CI = 1.00 to 10.53) compared with noncarriers.
Mutation carriers also had earlier age at onset of recurrent major depressive disorder than noncarriers.

notes.statement: Heiman et al. (2004) found that the severity of motor signs was not associated with the likelihood of recurrent depression. Carriers did not have a higher risk of other affective disorders, such as single major depression or bipolar disorder. The authors concluded that early-onset recurrent depression may be a clinical expression of the DYT1 GAG mutation, independent of motor manifestations.
quotes: The severity of motor signs was not associated with the likelihood of recurrent depression. Mutation carriers did not have an increased risk for other affective disorders, such as single major depression or bipolar disorder.
These findings suggest that early-onset recurrent depression is a clinical expression of the DYT1 gene mutation.

notes.statement: Using diffusion tensor MRI, Carbon et al. (2004) found reduced fractional anisotropy (p < 0.005) in the subgyral white matter of the sensorimotor cortex in DYT1 mutation carriers compared with control subjects. Fractional anisotropy is a measure of axonal integrity and coherence. The authors suggested that abnormal anatomical connectivity of the supplementary motor area may contribute to the susceptibility of DYT1 carriers to develop clinical manifestations of dystonia.
quotes: Fractional anisotropy (FA), a measure of axonal integrity and coherence, was reduced (p < 0.005) in the subgyral white matter of the sensorimotor cortex of DYT1 carriers.
Abnormal anatomical connectivity of the supplementary motor area may contribute to the susceptibility of DYT1 carriers to develop clinical manifestations of dystonia.

notes.statement: Carbon et al. (2004) used FDG PET to study 12 nonmanifesting and 11 manifesting DYT1 gene carriers, 6 nonmanifesting and 7 manifesting DYT6 gene carriers, and 11 controls. In both genotypes, manifesting carriers showed bilateral hypermetabolism in the presupplementary motor area (BA 6) and in the parietal association cortices (BA 40/7) compared with nonmanifesting carriers.
quotes: FDG PET was used to scan 12 nonmanifesting and 11 manifesting DYT1 gene carriers, 6 nonmanifesting DYT6 gene carriers and 7 manifesting DYT6 gene carriers, as well as 11 control subjects.

Manifesting gene carriers of both genotypes exhibited bilateral hypermetabolism in the presupplementary motor area (Brodmann area [BA] 6) and parietal association cortices (BA 40/7) compared with the respective nonmanifesting counterparts.

notes.statement: Carbon et al. (2004) found increased metabolism specific to DYT1 carriers in the putamen, anterior cingulate (BA 24/32), and cerebellar hemispheres. In contrast, DYT6 carriers showed putaminal hypometabolism and temporal cortex (BA 21) hypermetabolism. The authors concluded that clinical manifestations are related to cortical dysfunction, whereas subcortical metabolic abnormalities may be trait features specific to each dystonia genotype.
quotes: By contrast, genotype-specific increases in metabolism were found in the putamen, anterior cingulate (BA 24/32), and cerebellar hemispheres of DYT1 carriers. Genotype-specific changes in DYT6 involved hypometabolism of the putamen and hypermetabolism in the temporal cortex (BA 21).

Whereas clinical manifestations are related to cortical dysfunction, metabolic abnormalities in subcortical structures may represent trait features that are specific for individual dystonia genotypes.

notes.statement: Carbon et al. (2004) suggested that dystonia may be associated with abnormal movement preparation caused by defective sensorimotor integration.
quotes: Dystonia may be associated with abnormal movement preparation caused by defective sensorimotor integration.

notes.statement: ZEMAN et al. (1960) discussed formes frustes (incomplete or mild forms) of idiopathic dystonia musculorum deformans.
quotes: Idiopathic dystonia musculorum deformans. II. The formes frustes.

notes.statement: Grundmann et al. (2003) screened 256 unselected patients with various subtypes of dystonia from 4 movement disorder outpatient clinics in Germany and found the DYT1 GAG deletion in 6 (about 2.3%).
quotes: Two hundred fifty-six patients were tested for the GAG deletion mutation in the DYT1 gene
Six of the 256 patients did carry the GAG-deletion in the DYT1 gene.

notes.statement: Grundmann et al. (2003) found that only 2 of 6 DYT1 GAG deletion carriers had classic early-onset generalized dystonia, the others having multifocal dystonia or bilateral writer's cramp, and concluded that the mutation may be associated with segmental and multifocal forms, making a priori prediction of carrier status and genetic counseling difficult.
quotes: Our findings demonstrate that the mutation may be associated with not only generalized but also segmental and multifocal forms of dystonia.
A priori prediction of the mutation carrier status in dystonic patients and genetic counseling of affected families with respect to the clinical manifestation may prove difficult.

notes.statement: Ghilardi et al. (2003) compared motor performance and sequence learning in 12 clinically unaffected DYT1 mutation carriers and 12 age-matched controls. Movement time and spatial accuracy were similar in the two groups, but sequence learning was reduced in gene carriers (p less than 0.01).
quotes: we compared movement and sequence learning in 12 clinically unaffected DYT1 carriers with 12 age-matched controls

We found that motor performance was similar in the DYT1 and control groups, with no significant differences in movement time and spatial accuracy measured during each of the tasks. In contrast, sequence learning was reduced in gene carriers relative to controls (p < 0.01).

notes.statement: Using H2(15)O PET, Ghilardi et al. (2003) found increased activation in the left premotor cortex and right supplementary motor area with reduced activation in the posterior medial cerebellum during motor execution in nonmanifesting DYT1 carriers, and increased activation in the left ventral prefrontal cortex and lateral cerebellum during sequence learning. They suggested that localized increases in neural activity may enable normal movement execution but may not compensate for the sequence learning defect.
quotes: PET imaging during motor execution showed increased activation in gene carriers (p < 0.001, uncorrected) in the left premotor cortex and right supplementary motor area, with concomitant reduction in the posterior medial cerebellum.
During sequence learning, activation responses in DYT1 carriers were increased in the left ventral prefrontal cortex, and lateral cerebellum.
Although localized increases in neural activity may enable normal movement execution in these subjects, this mechanism may not compensate for their defect in sequence learning.

notes.statement: Bressman et al. (2002) assessed 147 DYT1 GAG deletion carriers and 113 blood-related noncarriers from 43 families. Only the category of definite dystonia was 100% specific. Probable dystonia was more common in carriers than in noncarriers, but possible dystonia was not.
quotes: The authors assessed 147 DYT1 GAG deletion carriers and 113 blood-related noncarriers from 43 families. Only the category of definite dystonia was 100% specific.
Probable dystonia, but not possible, was increased in carriers compared with noncarriers.

notes.statement: Bressman et al. (2002) recommended that only individuals with definite signs of dystonia be considered affected in linkage and other genetic studies of DYT1 families.
quotes: The authors recommend that only those with definite signs of dystonia be considered affected in linkage and other genetic studies.

notes.statement: Hjermind et al. (2002) found the DYT1 GAG deletion in only 3 of 107 Danish probands with primary torsion dystonia, a low frequency even though several probands had early-onset generalized dystonia. No proband with other types of dystonia carried the GAG deletion.
quotes: Mutation analyses for the GAG-deletion in the DYT1 gene were performed on 107 probands; and the mutation was detected in three.
The frequency of DYT1-dystonia was low in our study even though several probands had early onset generalised dystonia.
None of the probands in our study with other types of dystonia had the GAG-deletion as reported in other studies.

notes.statement: Hjermind et al. (2002) noted that de novo mutations in the DYT1 gene are seldom reported, although independent founder mutations are known to have occurred. They discussed how the heterogeneity of dystonia, as illustrated by DYT1 dystonia, makes genetic counseling difficult.
quotes: De novo mutations in the DYT1 gene are seldom reported although independent founder mutations are known to have occurred.
The difficulties in genetic counselling concerning the heterogeneity of dystonia exemplified by DYT1-dystonia are outlined.

notes.statement: Németh (2002) reviewed the genetics of dystonias. The review covered primary dystonias, including idiopathic torsion dystonia (DYT1), focal dystonias (DYT7) and mixed dystonias (DYT6 and DYT13), as well as the 'dystonia-plus' syndromes and heredodegenerative disorders.
quotes: Dystonias are a heterogeneous group of disorders which are known to have a strong inherited basis.
Conditions discussed in detail include idiopathic torsion dystonia (DYT1), focal dystonias (DYT7) and mixed dystonias (DYT6 and DYT13)

notes.statement: Leung et al. (2001) screened the TOR1A gene in 40 patients with early onset dystonia or early onset parkinsonism (EOP) and identified 3 variations, none in EOP patients. Two infrequent intronic single-bp changes of unknown consequence were found in a dystonia patient and in the mother of an EOP patient.
quotes: In a screen of 40 patients, we identified three variations, none of which occurred in EOP patients.
Two infrequent intronic single base pair (bp) changes of unknown consequences were found in a dystonia patient and the mother of an EOP patient.

notes.statement: Leung et al. (2001) found that the 18-bp deletion would remove 6 amino acids close to the C terminus of torsinA, including a putative phosphorylation site. It was the first TOR1A mutation identified other than the GAG deletion (Glu302/303del), and it was associated with a distinct type of early onset dystonia.
quotes: This deletion would remove 6 amino acids close to the carboxy terminus, including a putative phosphorylation site of torsinA.
This 18-bp deletion is the first additional mutation, beyond the GAG-deletion (Glu302/303del), to be found in the TOR1A gene, and is associated with a distinct type of early onset dystonia.

notes.statement: Valente et al. (1999) analyzed haplotypes surrounding DYT1 in 9 Ashkenazi Jewish and 15 non-Jewish British patients carrying the GAG deletion. All the British Ashkenazi Jewish patients carried the same haplotype as North American Ashkenazi Jews, supporting the idea that the British Ashkenazi Jewish community descends from the same small group of individuals as North American Jews.
quotes: we analysed the haplotypes surrounding DYT1 in 9 AJ and 15 non-Jewish British patients carrying the GAG deletion in the DYT1 gene

We found that all AJ British patients carried the same haplotype as the North American Jews, sustaining the theory that the current British AJ community descends from the same small group of individuals as the North American Jewry.

notes.statement: Valente et al. (1999) observed only a limited number of distinct founder haplotypes among non-Jewish British carriers of the GAG deletion. They concluded that the deletion is probably not a very frequent mutation and has arisen only a limited number of times over the centuries.
quotes: in the non-Jewish British patients, only a limited number of distinct founder mutations was observed. This supports the hypothesis that the GAG deletion in the DYT1 gene is not a very frequent mutation, and that it has arisen only a limited number of times throughout the centuries.

notes.statement: Müller et al. (1998) reviewed the clinical and molecular genetics of primary dystonias and proposed referring to the known forms, most of which can be distinguished by genetic criteria, as dystonias 1-12.
quotes: proposes referring to the known forms, most of which can be distinguished by genetic criteria, as dystonias 1-12

notes.statement: Müller et al. (1998) noted at least 8 clinically distinct autosomal dominant and 2 X-linked recessive forms of primary dystonia, with gene loci identified in at least 6 autosomal dominant forms, including idiopathic torsion dystonia at 9q34; mutations in a gene coding for an ATP-binding protein were detected in idiopathic torsion dystonia (DYT1).
quotes: There are at least eight clinically distinct autosomal dominant and two X-linked recessive forms.
To date gene loci have been identified in at least six autosomal dominant forms, i.e., in idiopathic torsion dystonia (9q34)
Mutations in a gene coding for an ATP-binding protein were detected in idiopathic torsion dystonia (DYT1)

notes.statement: Kamm et al. (1999) screened 57 German patients with idiopathic torsion dystonia for the 3-bp GAG deletion in the DYT1 gene and found it in 3 of 5 patients with early limb-onset ITD and in 1 young patient with multifocal dystonia. The mutation was absent in 2 patients with early-onset generalized dystonia beginning in the cervical muscles, 5 other multifocal, 14 segmental, and 30 focal cervical dystonia patients.
quotes: We examined 57 patients with idiopathic torsion dystonia (ITD) for the 3-bp GAG deletion in the DYT1 gene on human chromosome 9q34.

Two patients with early-onset generalized dystonia beginning in the cervical muscles, as well as five other patients with multifocal, 14 patients with segmental, and 30 patients with focal cervical dystonia did not carry the mutation.

notes.statement: Kamm et al. (1999) suggested that the GAG deletion is responsible for a major portion of typical early limb-onset dystonia, but not for other types of dystonia, in the German population.
quotes: This suggests that the GAG deletion is responsible for a major portion of cases of typical early limb-onset dystonia, but not for other types of dystonia, in our population.

notes.statement: Ozelius et al. (1997) described early-onset torsion dystonia as a movement disorder with twisting muscle contractures beginning in childhood, with symptoms believed to result from altered neuronal communication in the basal ganglia.
quotes: Early-onset torsion dystonia is a movement disorder, characterized by twisting muscle contractures, that begins in childhood. Symptoms are believed to result from altered neuronal communication in the basal ganglia.

notes.statement: Ozelius et al. (1997) identified the DYT1 gene on chromosome 9q34 as responsible for dominant early-onset torsion dystonia and found that almost all cases carried a unique 3-bp deletion causing loss of one of a pair of glutamic acid residues in a conserved region of torsinA.
quotes: This study identifies the DYT1 gene on human chromosome 9q34 as being responsible for this dominant disease.
This deletion results in loss of one of a pair of glutamic-acid residues in a conserved region of a novel ATP-binding protein, termed torsinA.

notes.statement: Ozelius et al. (1997) concluded that the recurrent 3-bp DYT1 deletion appeared to have arisen independently in different ethnic populations.
quotes: Almost all cases of early-onset dystonia have a unique 3-bp deletion that appears to have arisen idependently in different ethnic populations.

notes.statement: Ozelius et al. (1997) found that DYT1 encodes a novel ATP-binding protein, torsinA, with homologs in nematode, rat, mouse, and human and some resemblance to the heat-shock protein and Clp protease families.
quotes: This protein has homologues in nematode, rat, mouse and humans, with some resemblance to the family of heat-shock proteins and Clp proteases.

notes.statement: Ozelius et al. (1997) built a YAC contig covering 600 kb of the 9q34 region that includes D9S62a. Using several new polymorphic loci, they extended the linkage disequilibrium analysis of the Ashkenazi Jewish founder mutation. The most likely location of the DYT1 gene was a 150-kb region between D9S2161 and D9S63.
quotes: A YAC contig has now been created spanning 600 kb of this region including D9S62a.
The most likely location of the DYT1 gene is within a 150 kb region between the loci D9S2161 and D9S63.

notes.statement: Ozelius et al. (1997) stated that early-onset torsion dystonia is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with reduced penetrance of 30 to 40%.
quotes: This disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant mode with reduced penetrance (30%-40%).

notes.statement: Ozelius et al. (1997) stated that the DYT1 gene appears to cause most cases of early-onset torsion dystonia in both Ashkenazi Jewish and non-Jewish families.
quotes: The DYT1 gene, which maps to chromosome 9q34, appears to be responsible for most cases of early-onset torsion dystonia in both Ashkenazic Jewish (AJ) and non-Jewish families.

notes.statement: Cheng et al. (1996) studied 260 probands with idiopathic adult-onset cranial or cervical dystonia (mean age at onset 45.71 years). Forty-nine had a family history of dystonia or tremor in first- or second-degree relatives. In these 49 families, onset came an average of 21.25 years earlier in the second generation than in the first (p = 1.11 x 10(-8)). The authors suggested genetic anticipation, possibly from an unstable trinucleotide repeat.
quotes: we studied the age of onset and family history of 260 patients (probands) with idiopathic adult-onset dystonia (IAD), cranial or cervical.
Age of onset of clinical symptoms was earlier, by an average of 21.25 years, in the second generation than in the first generation.
These findings are most compatible with genetic anticipation and suggest that an unstable trinucleotide repeat is most likely involved in adult-onset primary cranial or cervical dystonia.

notes.statement: Cheng et al. (1996) found postural or action tremor often in patients with adult-onset dystonia and in their relatives. They proposed that tremor may be an integral part of the dystonia phenotype.
quotes: The significance of tremor as a part of clinical manifestation of dystonia was evidenced by a high frequency of postural or action tremor in patients and relatives.

notes.statement: Gasser et al. (1996) determined haplotypes at 5 marker loci closely linked to DYT1 on chromosome 9q in 10 Ashkenazi Jewish patients with focal hand dystonia (8 with musician's cramp, 2 with writer's cramp). None of the 20 chromosomes could be constructed as the founder haplotype, which is associated with more than 90% of generalized dystonia cases in this population, and the authors found no common haplotype. They concluded that these findings argued against a role for the DYT1 founder mutation in occupational hand dystonia.
quotes: Genetic haplotypes at five marker loci that are closely linked to the DYT1 gene on chromosome 9q were determined in 10 Ashkenazi Jewish patients with focal hand dystonia (eight with musician's cramp, two with writer's cramp).
The founder haplotype associated with > 90% of cases generalized dystonia in the Ashkenazi Jewish population could not be constructed from any of the twenty chromosomes.
These findings argue against a role for the founder mutation in the DYT1 gene in the etiology of occupational hand dystonia in this ethnic group.

notes.statement: Gasser et al. (1996) suggested that excessive, repetitive use, possibly together with ulnar neuropathy, may be the inciting cause of some focal dystonias. They also stated that if the DYT1 gene is involved in these later-onset dystonias, there was no evidence for a common mutation in the Ashkenazi Jewish population.
quotes: Further, if the DYT1 gene is involved in these later onset dystonias, there is no evidence for a common mutation in the Ashkenazic Jewish population.
It appears that excessive, repetitive use, possibly in combination with ulnar neuropathy, may serve as the inciting cause of some focal dystonias.

notes.statement: Warner et al. (1993) performed linkage analysis in 27 small families (26 British, 1 French) with idiopathic torsion dystonia, using the ASS and ABL loci on 9q34. The cumulative lod score for ASS at a recombination fraction of 0.001 was -6.72. HOMOG analysis nevertheless supported linkage to 9q34 in a subset of families, in both Jewish and non-Jewish kindreds in the UK.
quotes: The cumulative lod score for the more informative ASS locus at a recombination fraction of 0.001 was -6.72.
Analysis of all the data using HOMOG showed significant heterogeneity, but evidence for linkage of an idiopathic torsion dystonia gene to 9q34 in a subset of families.

notes.statement: Warner et al. (1993) found that in three non-Jewish families, clinically indistinguishable from the others, individual lod scores excluded a disease locus tightly linked to ASS on 9q34. The authors suggested genetic heterogeneity in idiopathic torsion dystonia.
quotes: A large component of this score was derived from three non-Jewish families, indistinguishable clinically from the others, in which individual lod scores excluded a disease locus tightly linked to ASS.
These data suggest genetic heterogeneity in idiopathic torsion dystonia

notes.statement: Warner et al. (1993) found that the allelic association between ASS/ABL and idiopathic torsion dystonia, previously seen in Ashkenazi families in the USA, was also present in British Jewish kindreds.
quotes: The allelic association observed between ASS/ABL and idiopathic torsion dystonia in Ashkenazi families in the USA was also present in British Jewish kindreds.

notes.statement: Kramer et al. (1994) found that linkage results in 7 non-Jewish families of northern European and French Canadian descent with early-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia were consistent with linkage to the DYT1 region on 9q34. Because none of them carried the Ashkenazi Jewish haplotype, the authors concluded that these families probably had different mutations in the DYT1 gene. The 2 French Canadian families shared the same haplotype.
quotes: Results are consistent with linkage to the DYT1 region.
None carries the AJ haplotype; therefore, they probably represent different mutations in the DYT1 gene. The two French Canadian families, however, display the same haplotype.

notes.statement: Kramer et al. (1994) estimated penetrance in non-Jewish DYT1 families at 0.40 to 0.75. After identifying disease gene carriers and adjusting for age at onset, they obtained a direct penetrance estimate of 0.46, consistent with estimates of 30 to 40% in the Ashkenazi Jewish population.
quotes: Estimates of penetrance in non-Jewish families range from .40 to .75. We identified disease gene carriers and, with adjustments for age at onset, obtained a direct estimate of penetrance of .46. This is consistent with estimates of 30%-40% in the AJ population.

notes.statement: Kramer et al. (1994) found that 2 other non-Jewish families with atypical idiopathic torsion dystonia (later onset and/or cranial or cervical involvement) were not linked to DYT1. They concluded that other genes are involved in dystonia.
quotes: Two other non-Jewish families with atypical ITD (later onset and/or cranial or cervical involvement) are not linked to DYT1, which indicates involvement of other genes in dystonia.

notes.statement: Kramer et al. (1994) noted that in the Ashkenazi Jewish population there was strong linkage disequilibrium between DYT1 and adjacent markers within a 2-cM region. The associated haplotype was present in more than 90% of early limb-onset Ashkenazi Jewish cases.
quotes: In the AJ population, strong linkage disequilibrium exists between DYT1 and adjacent markers within a 2-cM region. The associated haplotype occurs in > 90% of early limb-onset AJ cases.

notes.statement: Bressman et al. (1994) classified 174 Ashkenazi Jewish individuals with idiopathic torsion dystonia by 9q34 haplotype (D9S62, D9S63, ASS) and found 90 carriers of the DYT1-associated haplotype, 70 noncarriers, and 14 ambiguous. Noncarriers had later onset (mean 36.5 vs 12.5 years) and onset in the neck, larynx, or other cranial muscles in 79%, arm onset in 21%, and never leg onset.
quotes: We used GT(n) markers on chromosome 9q34 (D9S62, D9S63, and ASS) and classified individuals as having ("carriers"), not having ("noncarriers"), or being ambiguous with respect to a DYT1-associated haplotype.
In contrast, the neck, larynx, and other cranial muscles were the sites of onset in 79% of noncarriers; onset in the arms occurred in 21% and onset in the legs never occurred.

notes.statement: Bressman et al. (1994) found that limb onset, leg involvement during the course of disease, and age at onset distinguished DYT1 haplotype carriers from noncarriers with 90% accuracy.
quotes: Limb onset, leg involvement in the course of disease, and age at onset distinguished haplotype carriers from noncarriers with 90% accuracy.

notes.statement: Bressman et al. (1994) noted that linkage disequilibrium between DYT1 and a particular 9q34 haplotype in Ashkenazi Jews implies that a large proportion of early-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia in this population is due to a founder mutation in DYT1.
quotes: Further, there is linkage disequilibrium between DYT1 and a particular haplotype of alleles at 9q34 loci in this population. This implies that a large proportion of early-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia in Ashkenazi Jews is due to a founder mutation in DYT1.

notes.statement: Risch et al. (1995) used 6 closely linked microsatellite loci on 9q34 to study 59 Ashkenazi Jewish families with idiopathic torsion dystonia. They found that more than 90% of early-onset cases in the Ashkenazi population were due to a single founder mutation. They estimated that this mutation first appeared about 350 years ago.
quotes: Our data show that the vast majority (> 90%) of early-onset ITD cases in the Ashkenazi population are due to a single founder mutation, which we estimate first appeared approximately 350 years ago.

notes.statement: Risch et al. (1995) found that carriers of the founder mutation came mainly from the northern part of the historic Jewish Pale of settlement (Lithuania and Byelorussia). They estimated the current frequency of the mutation at between 1/6,000 and 1/2,000. The recent origin of this dominant mutation and its high frequency suggested that the Ashkenazi population descends from a limited group of founders, and that genetic drift has been important in determining disease allele frequencies in this population.
quotes: We also show that carriers preferentially originate from the northern part of the historic Jewish Pale of settlement (Lithuania and Byelorussia).
The recent origin of this dominant mutation and its current high frequency (between 1/6,000 and 1/2,000) suggest that the Ashkenazi population descends from a limited group of founders

notes.statement: Zoossmann-Diskin (1995) discussed whether genetic drift or selection accounts for idiopathic torsion dystonia (ITD) in Ashkenazi Jews.
quotes: ITD in Ashkenazi Jews--genetic drift or selection?

notes.statement: Askenasy et al. (1980) found significantly higher serum dopamine-beta-hydroxylase (DBH) activity in 13 Ashkenazi Jewish patients with torsion dystonia and in their relatives than in controls, especially in the childhood-onset group. None of the criteria of Jewish origin, dominant trait, slow progression, or axial topography were specific for elevated serum DBH activity.
quotes: A significantly high serum DBH activity was found in TD patients and their relatives compared with controls, particularly in the childhood onset group.
None of the following criteria: Jewish origin, dominant trait, slow progression and axial topography are specific for an elevated serum DBH activity.

notes.statement: Askenasy et al. (1980) found that intravenous metoclopramide (20 mg) did not change serum DBH activity in 12 patients and 17 relatives. In 1 patient with symptomatic dystonia and 2 of her maternal relatives, serum DBH activity doubled or tripled after the injection. The authors suggested that the metoclopramide-induced rise in DBH activity in relatives of patients indicated a genetic disposition.
quotes: Intravenous injection of 20 mg Metoclopramide (MP) did not change serum DBH activity in 12 patients and 17 relatives.

In one patient with symptomatic dystonia and two of her maternal relatives (from different fathers) serum DBH activity increased after i.v. injection of MP. In these three cases the serum DBH activity doubled and tripled.
It is suggested that the MP induced elevation of serum DBH activity in relatives of TD patients indicates a genetic disposition.

notes.statement: Eldridge (1981) discussed the inheritance of torsion dystonia in Jews.
quotes: Inheritance of torsion dystonia in Jews.

notes.statement: In a nationwide survey of idiopathic torsion dystonia in Israel, Zilber et al. (1984) found that the frequency in Jews of European origin was about 1 in 23,000 live births. This was five-fold greater than in Jews of Afro-Asian origin.
quotes: In these European Jews, the ITD frequency was about 1:23 000 live births, which was five-fold greater than in Jews of Afro-Asian origin.

notes.statement: Zilber et al. (1984) found that X-linked or simple autosomal recessive models did not fit their data well. An autosomal dominant model with low penetrance could account for the observations and gave an estimated gene frequency in European Jews of 3 to 4 per 100,000. Multifactorial inheritance was also possible, and the authors noted that not all cases need share the same genetic basis.
quotes: an X linked or a simple autosomal recessive model of inheritance did not agree well with our data. An autosomal dominant model with low penetrance could have accounted for our observations and would yield an ITD gene frequency in European Jews of 3 to 4:100 000.
Multifactorial inheritance was also possible. However, it may be inappropriate to assume that all cases have the same genetic basis, or even that all are inherited.

notes.statement: Zilber et al. (1984) observed increased paternal ages for isolated cases of torsion dystonia. They suggested that some of these cases may have been new mutations.
quotes: In view of the increased ages of their fathers, the isolated cases may have included some new mutations.

notes.statement: Lorden et al. (1984) described dystonic (dt), an autosomal recessive mutation in Sprague-Dawley rats. Signs began on postnatal day 10 and included twisting of the axial muscles, hyperflexion of the trunk, self-clasping of the limbs, and poor limb placement during walking. Routine light microscopy found no morphologic lesions in neural or non-neural tissue. The authors suggested that the dt rat may be a useful model for human dystonia musculorum deformans.
quotes: The mutation follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance and has been named dystonic (dt).

Clinical signs begin to appear on day 10 and include twisting of the axial musculature, hyperflexion of the trunk, self-clasping of forelimbs and hindlimbs, and poor placement of the limbs during locomotion.
The dt rat may provide a useful model for human dystonia musculorum deformans.

notes.statement: Lorden et al. (1984) found significantly raised norepinephrine levels in the cerebellum of dystonic rats. Norepinephrine levels in other locus ceruleus terminal fields were normal, and the noradrenergic innervation of the cerebellum looked normal. The mutant rats were less sensitive than their littermates to the akinesic effects of haloperidol, but their striatal dopamine levels and their response to apomorphine were normal. The authors suggested that these findings point to biochemical disturbances in the extrapyramidal system.
quotes: Dystonic rats demonstrate significantly elevated cerebellar norepinephrine levels, although levels in other terminal fields of the locus ceruleus are similar to those of normal littermates.
These mutants were less sensitive than unaffected littermates to the akinesic effects of the dopamine blocker haloperidol.
These findings suggest the presence of biochemical disturbances in the extrapyramidal system of dt rats.

notes.statement: Eldridge (1970) reviewed the literature on the torsion dystonias and presented genetic and clinical studies of these disorders.
quotes: The torsion dystonias: literature review and genetic and clinical studies.

notes.statement: Yanagisawa et al. (1972) reported familial dystonia musculorum deformans occurring together with tremor.
quotes: Familial dystonia musculorum deformans and tremor.

notes.statement: Wooten et al. (1973) reported elevated plasma dopamine-beta-hydroxylase activity in autosomal dominant torsion dystonia.
quotes: Elevated plasma dopamine-beta-hydroxylase activity in autosomal dominant torsion dystonia.

notes.statement: Batshaw et al. (1985) reported Munchausen syndrome simulating torsion dystonia, pointing to factitious disorder as part of the differential diagnosis of torsion dystonia.
quotes: Munchausen's syndrome simulating torsion dystonia.

notes.statement: Kramer et al. (1987) performed multipoint linkage analysis in a single large non-Jewish pedigree with autosomal dominant torsion dystonia and excluded linkage to large portions of chromosomes 11p and 13q and virtually the entire long arm of chromosome 21.
quotes: Large portions of chromosomes 11p and 13q, and virtually the entire long arm of chromosome 21 are excluded from linkage with dystonia.

notes.statement: Breakefield et al. (1986) carried out linkage analysis with RFLPs in a family with autosomal dominant torsion dystonia. They excluded the pro-opiomelanocortin and glutamic acid decarboxylase genes, which had been implicated in rat models, as the cause of the disease in this family. Other regions of the genome were also excluded.
quotes: Genes for pro-opiomelanocortin and glutamic acid decarboxylase, which have been implicated in the etiology of the disease in rat models, were excluded as being responsible for the disease state in this family.
Other regions of the genome were also excluded using DNA probes for other genes and random "unique" sequences.

notes.statement: Breakefield et al. (1986) analyzed linkage by the LOD score method. Their model assumed autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance and allowed for age of onset.
quotes: Linkage analysis, using cloned DNA sequences and restriction fragment length polymorphisms, was evaluated by the LOD score method with requisite assumptions for mode of inheritance, age-of-onset and incomplete gene penetrance.

notes.statement: In a study of 43 Ashkenazi Jewish probands with idiopathic torsion dystonia and their relatives, Bressman et al. (1989) found that the age-adjusted risk was 15.5% for first-degree relatives and 6.5% for second-degree relatives, counting definite cases only. They found no significant difference between the sexes and no significant difference among the risks to parents, offspring and sibs. The risks were consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance, with an estimated penetrance of 29.4% (definite cases only) or 32.2% (definite and probable cases).
quotes: Using definite cases only, the age-adjusted risk for all first-degree relatives was 15.5% and for all second-degree relatives 6.5%, with no significant sex differences; parent, offspring, and sibling risks did not differ significantly.
The risks were consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with a penetrance estimated at 29.4% using definite cases only or 32.2% using definite and probable cases.

notes.statement: Bressman et al. (1989) assumed a disease frequency of 1 in 15,000 among Ashkenazi Jews and estimated the gene frequency at 1 in 9,000.
quotes: Assuming a disease frequency of 1/15,000, the gene frequency was estimated to be 1/9000.

notes.statement: Ozelius et al. (1989) mapped a torsion dystonia susceptibility gene (ITD1) in a large non-Jewish kinship and found tight linkage to the gelsolin gene; multipoint linkage analysis placed it in 9q32-q34 between ABO and D9S26. The dopamine-beta-hydroxylase locus also lies in this region.
quotes: This dystonia gene (ITD1) shows tight linkage with the gene encoding gelsolin, an actin binding protein, and appears by multipoint linkage analysis to lie in the q32-q34 region of chromosome 9 between ABO and D9S26, a region that also contains the locus for dopamine-beta-hydroxylase.

notes.statement: Ozelius et al. (1989) stated that the defective torsion dystonia gene frequency in the Ashkenazi Jewish population is about 1/10,000.
quotes: In the Ashkenazi Jewish population the defective gene frequency is about 1/10,000.

notes.statement: Ozelius et al. (1989) described torsion dystonia as a movement disorder in which control of voluntary movements is lost, appearing as sustained muscle contractions and/or abnormal postures. They noted that most hereditary forms show autosomal dominant transmission with variable expressivity.
quotes: Torsion dystonia is a movement disorder of unknown etiology characterized by loss of control of voluntary movements appearing as sustained muscle contractions and/or abnormal postures.
Several hereditary forms have been described, most of which have autosomal dominant transmission with variable expressivity.

notes.statement: Hornykiewicz et al. (1986) studied the brains of 2 patients with generalized childhood-onset dystonia musculorum deformans after death. They found no important histologic changes. Choline acetyltransferase activity and GABA and glutamate levels were normal. Norepinephrine was markedly and consistently decreased in the lateral and posterior hypothalamus, mamillary body, subthalamic nucleus, and locus ceruleus. The authors suggested that a disturbance of noradrenergic brain mechanisms may be a basic neurochemical abnormality in the disorder.
quotes: Similarly, the activity of choline acetyltransferase and the levels of gamma-aminobutyric acid and glutamic acid in the cerebral cortex and basal ganglia were within the control range.
In contrast, the norepinephrine concentrations were markedly and consistently decreased in the lateral and posterior hypothalamus, mamillary body, subthalamic nucleus, and locus ceruleus.

We conclude that some of these monoamine changes, especially the pronounced apparent disturbance of noradrenergic brain mechanisms, may represent a basic neurochemical abnormality in dystonia musculorum deformans

notes.statement: Hornykiewicz et al. (1986) also found raised concentrations of norepinephrine in the septum, thalamus, colliculi, red nucleus, and dorsal raphe nucleus. Serotonin was elevated in the globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, and locus ceruleus. Homovanillic acid levels showed little consistent change.
quotes: Elevated concentrations of norepinephrine were found in the septum, thalamus, colliculi, red nucleus, and dorsal raphe nucleus; of serotonin, in the globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, and locus ceruleus;
The level of homovanillic acid showed little consistent change in the regions examined.

notes.statement: In a review, Müller and Kupke (1990) noted that primary torsion dystonia may be inherited as an autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked recessive trait. They stated that at least six forms of autosomal dominant torsion dystonia can be distinguished clinically.
quotes: The disorder may be inherited either as an autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked recessive trait. At least six forms of autosomal dominant torsion dystonia can be distinguished clinically.

notes.statement: Müller and Kupke (1990) reviewed linkage analysis in one form of autosomal dominant torsion dystonia, which assigned a torsion dystonia locus to the long arm of chromosome 9.
quotes: Linkage analysis in one form of autosomal dominant torsion dystonia permits the assignment of a "torsion dystonia locus" to the long arm of chromosome 9.

notes.statement: Müller and Kupke (1990) described primary torsion dystonia as an idiopathic movement disorder presumably caused by abnormal function of the basal ganglia.
quotes: Primary torsion dystonia is an idiopathic movement disorder presumably caused by abnormal function of the basal ganglia.

notes.statement: By linkage analysis with DNA polymorphisms in 12 Ashkenazi Jewish families with idiopathic torsion dystonia, Kramer et al. (1990) found close linkage of the dystonia gene to the argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS) gene; multipoint analysis placed it in 9q32-34, a region also containing the gelsolin and dopamine-beta-hydroxylase loci.
quotes: This dystonia gene exhibits close linkage with the gene encoding argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS), and appears by multipoint analysis to lie in the q32-34 region of chromosome 9, a region that also contains the loci for gelsolin and dopamine-beta-hydroxylase.

notes.statement: Kramer et al. (1990) suggested that the same gene may cause ITD in a previously mapped non-Jewish kindred and in Ashkenazi Jewish families, but because penetrance differed substantially between the groups, two different mutations may be operating.
quotes: The same gene may be responsible for ITD both in the non-Jewish kindred mentioned above and in the Ashkenazi Jewish families presented here. However, because there is substantial difference between the penetrance of the dominant allele in these two groups, two different mutations may be operating

notes.statement: Kramer et al. (1990) noted that the frequency of ITD in the Ashkenazi Jewish population is 5 to 10 times greater than in other groups.
quotes: The frequency of ITD in the Ashkenazi Jewish population is five to ten times greater than that in other groups.

notes.statement: Kramer et al. (1990) stated that most familial forms of ITD follow autosomal dominant transmission with reduced penetrance.
quotes: Most familial forms of ITD follow autosomal dominant transmission with reduced penetrance.

notes.statement: Risch et al. (1990) performed segregation analysis in a family study of idiopathic torsion dystonia in Ashkenazi Jews (43 probands with onset before age 27 years from 42 nuclear families) and found the data consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with 30% penetrance. Recessive and polygenic inheritance were strongly rejected, and there was no evidence for sporadic cases or new mutations.
quotes: Segregation analysis demonstrated that the data are consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with 30% penetrance. Recessive and polygenic inheritance were strongly rejected. There was no evidence for sporadic cases or new mutations.

notes.statement: Risch et al. (1990) suggested that the high incidence and dominant inheritance of early-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia in Ashkenazi Jews indicate genetic homogeneity within this population, making it especially useful for linkage studies.
quotes: The high incidence and dominant inheritance of early-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia in Ashkenazi Jews suggests genetic homogeneity within this population, making it especially useful for linkage studies of this disorder.

notes.statement: Using GT repeat polymorphisms, Kwiatkowski et al. (1991) localized the dystonia gene in Ashkenazi Jewish families to the 11-cM interval between AK1 and D9S10 on 9q32-34. Linkage analysis in a large non-Jewish family was also consistent with the gene lying in this region, although in that family positive lod scores extended over more than 20 cM.
quotes: Utilizing GT repeat polymorphisms from this region, here we demonstrate that the gene causing dystonia in Ashkenazi Jews can be localized to the 11-cM interval between AK1 and D9S10.
Linkage analysis in the non-Jewish family is also consistent with occurrence of the gene in this region, although positive lod scores extend over a greater than 20-cM interval in that family.

notes.statement: Kwiatkowski et al. (1991) described idiopathic torsion dystonia as characterized by sustained, involuntary muscle contractions that frequently cause twisting and repetitive movements or abnormal postures. They noted that most familial forms show autosomal dominant inheritance with reduced penetrance.
quotes: Idiopathic torsion dystonia (ITD) is characterized by sustained, involuntary muscle contractions, frequently causing twisting and repetitive movements or abnormal postures.
Most familial forms of ITD display autosomal dominant inheritance with reduced penetrance.

notes.statement: Ozelius et al. (1992) identified obligate recombination events in Ashkenazi Jewish families that narrowed the DYT1 region on chromosome 9q to a 6-cM interval bounded by AK1 and ASS, with DYT1 centromeric to ASS.
quotes: we have identified obligate recombination events in some of these Jewish families, which further delineate the area containing the DYT1 gene to a 6-cM region bounded by loci AK1 and ASS.
on the basis of obligate recombination events, the DYT1 gene is centromeric to ASS.

notes.statement: Ozelius et al. (1992) found strong linkage disequilibrium between DYT1 and an extended ABL-ASS haplotype (4/A12), present on 69% of disease-bearing chromosomes in affected Ashkenazi Jews but only 1% of control Jewish chromosomes, suggesting that a single mutation event accounts for most hereditary dystonia in this population and that DYT1 lies within 1-2 cM of these loci.
quotes: The 4/A12 haplotype for ABL-ASS is present on 69% of the disease-bearing chromosomes among affected Jewish individuals and on only 1% of control Jewish chromosomes (chi 2 = 91.07, P much less than .001).
this allelic association supports the idea that a single mutation event is responsible for most hereditary cases of dystonia in the Jewish population.

notes.statement: Ozelius et al. (1992) found that sporadic cases carried the ASS A12 allele at a similar rate (8/13) to familial cases (28/40), suggesting that many sporadic cases are hereditary, that the disease gene frequency in Ashkenazi Jews exceeds 1/15,000, and that penetrance is lower than 30%.
quotes: the proportion of sporadic cases which potentially carry the A12 haplotype at ASS (8/13 [62%]) is similar to the proportion of familial cases with A12 (28/40 [70%]).
This suggests that many sporadic cases are hereditary, that the disease gene frequency is greater than 1/15,000, and that the penetrance is lower than 30%

notes.statement: Ozelius et al. (1992) found that most affected individuals were heterozygous for the ABL-ASS haplotype, supporting autosomal dominant inheritance of DYT1.
quotes: Most affected individuals were heterozygous for the ABL-ASS haplotype, a finding supporting autosomal dominant inheritance of the DYT1 gene.

notes.statement: Ozelius et al. (1992) proposed that ABL-ASS extended-haplotype status could predict carrier status in Jewish individuals and be used for molecular diagnosis.
quotes: The ABL-ASS extended-haplotype status will provide predictive value for carrier status in Jewish individuals. This information can be used for molecular diagnosis

notes.statement: Bundey et al. (1975) found at least two clinically indistinguishable forms of generalized childhood-onset torsion dystonia, one autosomal dominant and one autosomal recessive. They concluded that the dominant forms could begin in childhood or in adult life.
quotes: These two forms, an autosomal dominant and an autosomal recessive, are clinically indistinguishable.
one or more dominant forms, with onset in childhood or adult life

notes.statement: Bundey et al. (1975) estimated that fitness in childhood-onset dystonia was 1/20 of normal, so most childhood-onset dominant cases appeared sporadically. Because of a probable paternal age effect, they thought 9 to 11 sporadic patients with generalized childhood dystonia represented new dominant mutations.
quotes: The remaining nine to 11 patients with generalized childhood dystonia are thought, because of a probable paternal age effect, to be examples of new dominant mutations.
Since fitness with childhood onset is 1/20 of normal, most childhood dominant cases appear sporadically.

notes.statement: Bundey et al. (1975) identified an autosomal recessive childhood-onset form of torsion dystonia in at least 3 families, probably involving about 6 to 8 patients. They suggested, on American evidence, that this form is particularly common in Ashkenazi Jews. They concluded that most isolated adult-onset cases seemed to have exogenous but unidentified causes.
quotes: There were at least three families and probably about six to eight patients with the autosomal recessive variety.
an autosomal recessive form with onset in childhood, which, on evidence from America, is particularly common in Ashkenazi Jews
The majority of adult-onset isolated cases of idiopathic torsion dystonia seem to be due to exogenous but unidentified causes.

notes.statement: Ziegler et al. (1976) studied plasma norepinephrine and dopamine-beta-hydroxylase levels in patients with dystonia.
quotes: Plasma norepinephrine and dopamine-beta-hydroxylase in dystonia.

notes.statement: Marsden et al. (1976) reported on the natural history of idiopathic torsion dystonia.
quotes: Natural history of idiopathic torsion dystonia.
